item.text:
The HVAC demand flexibility measures are **upgrades 24–28** in ResStock 2025 Release 1. They differ in **when the thermostat changes, how long it changes, and the temperature offset**. The release’s [Upgrade Measures page](https://natlabrockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/docs/upgrade_measures.html) lists all five:

| Upgrade | Strategy | Duration of thermostat change | Offset |
|---|---|---|---|
| **24** | On-peak load shedding | 4 hours during peak | 2°F |
| **25** | Pre-peak load shifting | 4 hours before peak | 2°F |
| **26** | On-peak load shedding | 4 hours during peak | 4°F |
| **27** | Pre-peak load shifting | 4 hours before peak | 4°F |
| **28** | Pre-peak load shifting | 1 hour before peak | 2°F |

Durations and offsets are confirmed in **Table 8, printed page 25**, of [*ResStock Measure Documentation: HVAC Load Flexibility*](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf#page=33).

**Load shedding (24 and 26)** lowers the heating setpoint or raises the cooling setpoint during peak hours, allowing indoor temperatures to drift to reduce demand. Neither includes preconditioning. Upgrade 26 doubles upgrade 24’s offset.

**Load shifting (25, 27, and 28)** preheats or precools the home before peak hours, using the building’s thermal mass to reduce subsequent demand. These have no on-peak setpoint adjustment. Upgrade 27 doubles upgrade 25’s offset; upgrade 28 shortens upgrade 25’s preconditioning from four hours to one. The final scenarios keep shifting and shedding separate. See [report §1.2.1–1.2.2 and §4.4](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf).

One modeling caveat: dispatch occurs nearly every day to estimate technical potential. The report cautions against interpreting annual energy savings as a realistic demand-response program outcome. See [§1.2.5, printed page 7](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf#page=15).
